# The Physical Cost of Context: Quality-Constrained Resource Accounting for Coding Agents

**Authors:** Zhongming Yu Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Yitong Ma Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Hengjia Yu Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Boqin Yuan Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Xiangye Lin Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst Hejia Zhang Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Jishen Zhao Affiliation: University of California, San Diego

## Abstract

Coding agents resend a growing context on every model call, and context policies are usually judged by the prompt tokens they save. Executed work also depends on call count and prefix reuse: a caching runtime prefills only the tokens after the longest cached prefix. A shorter prompt can therefore cost more if it rewrites cached history. Our quality-gated protocol splits executed prefill into logical prompt minus reused prefix and measures KV residency, time, and energy. On 450 localization cases derived from SWE-rebench V2, preloading ten retrieved blocks (Eager) and adding anchored history compaction (Compact) both pass a five-point non-inferiority gate. In a separate 900-cell study, Eager cuts model calls by 35.7% and the GPU-energy proxy by 33.2% against on-demand search (Grep); Compact saves nothing further. Enabling prefix caching leaves Eager’s prompt volume similar ( $+8.3\%$ ; its 95% CI spans zero) but cuts its uncached prefill by 67.7%. Deleting history can turn a token saving into extra work. With mini-SWE-agent on 100 SWE-bench Verified instances, keeping only the last five observations (Mask-5) cuts Eager’s prompt volume by 33.3% but loses 135.9k reusable tokens per task. Uncached prefill rises by 608.5%, the energy proxy by 125.6%, and the policy misses the quality gate. Policies thus save physical work by shortening the trajectory and can multiply it by editing reusable history.

## 1 Introduction

Repository localization maps an issue report to files, classes, and functions. Retrieval methods rank files using report–code similarity, structure, and history [1, 2, 3]. Modern agents combine iterative retrieval [4], structure-aware search [5, 6, 7], or graph navigation [8, 9, 10, 11].

These agents repeatedly search, read, and reassess the retrieved source. A ReAct-style loop [12] turns a short issue report into a trajectory of tool outputs and intermediate hypotheses. Larger contexts may improve evidence coverage, but every retained observation can add input processing before decoding (prefill) and occupy the model’s key–value (KV) cache on later turns. On a local device, model weights, KV cache, retrieval services, and the host process also share one memory and power budget.

Many context-management studies report tokens, task success, or provider cost [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. Token counts do not determine physical cost: equal reductions in logical tokens can correspond to different amounts of executed prefill, depending on request boundaries and prefix reuse [18, 19]. On a unified-memory device, model and host allocations also share one pool [20], so we track host allocation, paging, and latency together.

Our agent returns answer blocks for an issue-like query. A frozen retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) path can insert ten retrieved code blocks before the first turn. We ask when logical-token savings predict physical savings, and when cache or trajectory effects break that prediction.

(c) Request and prefix-reuse boundaries translate logical prompt $P$ into uncached work $U$ and device cost, which we compare only after checking quality.*

Measuring this path (Figure 1) raises three challenges. C1: Trajectory attribution. Evidence supply, delivery time, and history retention can each change what the agent does next. Matched contrasts hold the other mechanisms fixed, and we treat the resulting trajectory as an outcome of the policy. C2: Logical-to-physical translation. A policy changes both the number of requests and prefix reuse within each request. Logical tokens can therefore order policies differently from uncached prefill, KV occupancy, latency, or energy. C3: Quality-constrained comparison. A resource comparison must first bound task-quality loss.

We study four fixed context policies on an NVIDIA DGX Spark: Grep, Eager, Compact, and Mask-5. They differ in when retrieved evidence arrives and which observations stay visible. We make two contributions:

- 1. A quality-gated physical-accounting protocol. The protocol combines paired task-quality bounds with model calls, uncached prefill, KV time-area, wall time, and idle-subtracted GPU energy. It charges failures, reports index construction separately, and decomposes executed prefill into logical input minus reused prefixes.

- 2. A controlled policy analysis. Byte-identical candidates separate evidence delivery from history reduction. On 450 real-issue localization cases derived from SWE-rebench V2, both preload policies satisfy the quality gate. Instrumented runs show that eager evidence saves work by avoiding calls, anchored reduction adds no saving beyond Eager, and repeated observation masking can erase prompt savings, consistent with reduced prefix reuse.

## 2 Context as a Resource-Control Problem

### 2.1 Two Paths from Context to Cost

A context policy changes both the requests an agent makes and the prefixes its runtime can reuse. Serving runtimes such as vLLM and SGLang keep the KV entries of earlier requests; when a new request begins with a cached token prefix, the runtime reuses those entries and prefills only the remaining suffix [21, 22]. Editing an early token therefore forces every later token to be recomputed. Let $n_{p}$ be the number of model requests under policy $p$ , $\ell_{p,t}$ the logical prompt tokens in request $t$ , and $h_{p,t}$ the tokens served from a reusable prefix. Aggregate logical and executed input work satisfy

$$ T_{\mathrm{prompt}}(p)=\sum_{t=1}^{n_{p}}\ell_{p,t},\qquad T_{\mathrm{uncached}}(p)=T_{\mathrm{prompt}}(p)-\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{n_{p}}h_{p,t}}_{T_{\mathrm{hit}}(p)}. $$

For a treatment–control contrast, $\Delta T_{\mathrm{uncached}}=\Delta T_{\mathrm{prompt}}-\Delta T_{\mathrm{hit}}$ . Prompt savings therefore increase executed prefill when a policy loses more reusable tokens than it removes. Because $n_{p}$ also depends on the policy, fewer calls can reduce total work even when each call is no cheaper. We use this decomposition to distinguish trajectory effects from runtime-reuse effects.

### 2.2 Frozen Code-RAG Supply Path

Following RAG [23], each snapshot is compiled offline into CodeNib function/class blocks [24] and encoded by a revision-pinned Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model [25]. The same encoder maps the issue query, and dense search returns ten spans. We exclude lexical fusion, graph expansion, and reranking.

Query encoding and search count toward each preload task; compilation is amortized separately. Hashes verify byte-identical preload inputs, and Grep keeps the same tools without a seed (Figure 1a–b).

### 2.3 Policy Algebra

Let $\sigma\in\{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{patch}\}$ identify the agent scaffold. For scaffold $\sigma$ , let $S_{\sigma}$ be its system prompt and $H_{\sigma,t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t},o_{t})$ its canonical action–observation history. An experimental arm is $p=(\sigma,e,r)$ , where $e\in\{\varnothing,R_{10}\}$ is the evidence supplied before the first turn and $r$ controls visible serialization. With $M_{E}$ denoting the compiled repository index and $R_{10}=R_{10}(q;M_{E})$ , the visible state and the serialized model input are

$$ V_{\sigma,t}^{(e)}=q\oplus e\oplus H_{\sigma,t},\qquad P_{\sigma,t}^{(e,r)}=S_{\sigma}\oplus r\!\left(V_{\sigma,t}^{(e)}\right), $$

where $\oplus$ denotes serialization. Policies retain the raw $H_{\sigma,t}$ for audit and change only its model-visible serialization.

Three deterministic context-serialization operators cover the tested designs:

$$ \displaystyle I\!\left(V_{\sigma,t}^{(e)}\right) \displaystyle=V_{\sigma,t}^{(e)}, \displaystyle A_{\sigma}\!\left(V_{\sigma,t}^{(R_{10})}\right) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}V_{\sigma,t}^{(R_{10})},&t<\tau,\\
D_{\tau,\sigma}\oplus H_{\sigma,\tau+1:t},&t\geq\tau,\end{cases} \displaystyle L_{5}\!\left(V_{\mathrm{patch},t}^{(R_{10})}\right) \displaystyle=q\oplus R_{10}\oplus H_{\mathrm{patch},t}\!\left[o_{i}\leftarrow\mu(|o_{i}|)\ \text{for }i\leq t-5\right]. $$

Here $\tau$ is the first successful source read. The scaffold-specific anchor $D_{\tau,\sigma}$ contains the task query exactly once, the successful read, and a bounded pre-rewrite assessment. Following SWE-agent’s LastNObservations [26], $L_{5}$ keeps actions and tool IDs but replaces older outputs with line-count markers. Neither invokes a model. $A_{\sigma}$ rewrites once; $L_{5}$ rewrites whenever an observation leaves the window. Both can change later actions and invalidate reuse, so total saving depends on $n_{p}$ and $T_{\mathrm{hit}}(p)$ in Equation (1).

The arm definitions are therefore

$$ \displaystyle G \displaystyle=(\mathrm{loc},\varnothing,I), \displaystyle N \displaystyle=(\mathrm{patch},\varnothing,I), \displaystyle E_{\sigma} \displaystyle=(\sigma,R_{10},I), \displaystyle C_{\sigma} \displaystyle=(\sigma,R_{10},A_{\sigma}), \displaystyle M_{5} \displaystyle=(\mathrm{patch},R_{10},L_{5}). $$

Thus $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{loc}}=\{G,E_{\mathrm{loc}},C_{\mathrm{loc}}\}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{patch}}=\{N,E_{\mathrm{patch}},C_{\mathrm{patch}},M_{5}\}$ . Informally, Grep ( $G$ , localization) and native mini-SWE-agent ( $N$ , patching) start from the issue alone and keep their full history. Eager ( $E_{\sigma}$ ) prepends the ten retrieved spans and also keeps the full history. Compact ( $C_{\sigma}$ ) matches Eager until the first successful source read, then replaces the candidate list and exploratory history with a short anchor. Mask-5 ( $M_{5}$ ) keeps every action but shortens each tool output older than the latest five to a placeholder, so once the window fills, every request rewrites an observation that the previous request had already sent. Within a study, seeded arms receive byte-identical $R_{10}$ . The $C_{\sigma}-E_{\sigma}$ contrast estimates the end-to-end effect of the anchor rewrite; $M_{5}-E_{\mathrm{patch}}$ estimates masking. Contrasts against $G$ or $N$ also add the retrieved evidence, so they combine delivery with any retention change. We do not pool absolute resources across Tables 1 and 2.

### 2.4 Quality-Constrained Resource Objective

For each gated treatment $p$ , let $Q(p)$ denote its task-quality endpoint and let $c(p)$ denote its registered control. We use answer-block Recall@5 for localization and official resolved rate for patch generation. Let

$$ \mathbf{R}(p)=(T_{\mathrm{prompt}},T_{\mathrm{output}},N_{\mathrm{req}},T_{\mathrm{uncached}},L_{\mathrm{TTFT}},L_{\mathrm{wall}},K_{\int},K_{\max},U_{\max},E_{\mathrm{gpu}}) $$

collect logical prompt and output tokens, requests, uncached-prefill tokens, time to first token, wall time, integrated and peak KV occupancy, peak unified-memory pressure, and sampled GPU energy. Here $K_{\int}$ , the KV time-area, integrates allocated KV bytes over wall time (GiB $\cdot$ s); unlike $K_{\max}$ , it does not let one long failed request define an arm. With $\operatorname{LCB}_{.95}$ denoting the lower endpoint of a paired 95% interval obtained by resampling whole repositories, a policy is eligible only if

$$ \operatorname{LCB}_{.95}\!\left[Q(p)-Q(c(p))\right]>-\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon=0.05. $$

The control is Grep for the two localization treatments and Eager for the Mask-5 patch contrast. The constraint is applied after each experiment to decide which policies enter the cost comparison; it does not act at runtime. Failed tasks remain in denominators and server resource totals, including requests without a serialized cell. We also report cost per successful endpoint so a cheap failure does not appear efficient.

## 3 Evaluation

#### Questions.

The RQs map to Section 1. RQ1 (C1/C3) asks which delivery and retention policies satisfy the quality gate and how they change the agent trajectory. RQ2 (C2) asks when the logical-token ordering survives translation into prefill, KV occupancy, latency, memory, and energy. A same-model prefix-cache intervention isolates prefix reuse. RQ3 (C1/C3) tests whether the token–work relationship recurs in an external agent scaffold with official patch grading.

#### Localization Cohorts.

Two disjoint cohorts share the CodeNib runner, retriever, policies, model, and Recall@5 endpoint. The synthesis cohort supports repeated device measurement; the SWE-rebench-derived cohort powers the quality gate.

The resource cohort comes from the frozen codenib-synthesis test split [24]. It contains 25 pinned repository snapshots, five each for Python, Go, Rust, TypeScript/JavaScript, and C/C++. Category-balanced round robin selects four of six issue-like query types per snapshot: behavioral, file hint, module hint, symbol hint, reasoning, and traversal. The resulting 100 tasks have function/class answer blocks for Recall@5; three policy repetitions produce 900 cells. Bootstrap draws retain each repository’s tasks, repetitions, and policy outcomes: the 300 cells per arm form 25 independent groups. The dataset labels its queries LLM-curated and LLM-judged but omits both model identifiers; we make no claim about human-authored issue distributions.

The powered quality cohort is derived from SWE-rebench V2 [27], a public GitHub issue–patch collection. Before model calls, we select 450 Python issues from distinct repositories. Eligible cases have an applicable gold patch, at most 5,000 tracked Python files, and a base-visible function/class block touched by the patch. We use those blocks as localization targets, separately from the SWE-bench Verified patch study. Variance from the 100-task instrumented pilot gives a maximum requirement of 441 independent cases, rounded to 450. One run per policy yields 1,350 cells and powers quality only; physical costs use the 100-task cohort. We do not pool the cohorts.

#### Localization Stack and Host.

All localization studies, comprising the 450-instance quality cohort, 900-cell resource matrix, and cache intervention, use the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 revision (35B total, 3B active) [28] with vLLM [21]. We set temperature to zero, cap context at 65,536 tokens, and admit one measured request at a time. Prefix caching is disabled in the resource matrix; the mechanism study toggles only that flag. A revision-pinned Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B server supplies every dense top-10. The host is a DGX Spark with an NVIDIA GB10 SoC and 128 GB coherent unified memory [20]. Appendix A records exact revisions, serving versions, memory reservations, and telemetry metadata.

#### Cache Mechanism Study.

RQ2 toggles one vLLM prefix-cache flag over the same 100 localization tasks. Model, runtime, decoder, task order, and revision remain fixed, yielding 600 cells and 25 paired repositories per policy and regime. Resets and salts restrict reuse to each four-query block; an audit confirms that the serving commands of the two regimes differ only in that flag.

#### External Patch Study and Stack Boundary.

A repository-balanced seeded hash selects 100 SWE-bench Verified instances across all 12 Python repositories [29, 30], without inspecting gold patches, tests, or outcomes. Mini-SWE-agent [31] v2.4.6 uses its official prompt, bash interface, and submission protocol. A separately deployed SGLang RadixAttention stack [22] uses DFlash speculative decoding with eight draft tokens [32]; Appendix A gives both checkpoint revisions. We compare Mini, Eager, Compact, and Mask-5; the three seeded arms receive identical top-10 candidates. Each arm gets one trajectory, 32 calls, 1,800 seconds, temperature zero, and no reference-patch access. The stricter-than-upstream call cap makes resolved rate a fixed-budget endpoint.

The external target and serving stack differ from localization, so we compare policies only within each stack. This study tests whether the pattern recurs; it cannot separate the effects of target model, scaffold, and runtime.

The revision-pinned official harness scores every attempt. Empty patches and failures remain in the denominator. Generation and retrieval enter resource totals; AMD64 grading does not. Eight shards repeat each arm order twice, with a Radix-cache reset per policy–shard block.

#### Controls.

Localization arms share the base prompt, tools, 16-turn limit, and decoder. A repository-level Latin square interleaves repetitions. The patch study uses the declared four-arm rotation. Each measured block follows an unmeasured warm-up and idle window; failed requests remain charged.

#### Measurements.

Agent traces provide prompt tokens, completion, calls, and wall time. Server counters provide generation, prefill, TTFT, latency, and KV usage. We report successful server calls per attempted task; “per call” always divides by that server counter. One-second KV sampling gives time-integrated occupancy; SGLang counters also separate device hits from uncached prefill and confirm DFlash activity. We compute the GPU-energy proxy by trapezoidally integrating sampled nvidia-smi power.draw over the run and subtracting the pre-run mean idle power multiplied by the run duration. It is not whole-system energy. Unified host memory comes from /proc/meminfo and cgroups. Prompt, wall time, and agent calls are per cell. Server counters, KV time-area, and power are aggregated per policy–shard block in the primary and external patch studies, and per policy–repository block in the same-model cache study.

#### Analysis.

Full answer-block Recall@5 defines localization success. A 10,000-draw paired bootstrap averages repetitions and resamples 25 repository groups. The 450-case cohort has one instance per repository, so its two resampling views coincide; SWE-bench draws instead resample 12 source repositories. Wall-time intervals use 25 groups. Block-level counters resample three disjoint shards while retaining repetitions. The instrumented study lacked prospective power analysis. We report build cost separately as $C_{\mathrm{build}}/n$ .

Across 450 localization cases derived from SWE-rebench V2, one per repository, the frozen retriever reaches .431 Recall@5 and .548 Recall@10. Agent Recall@5 is .470, .478, and .494 for Grep, Eager, and Compact (Table 1). Nonconforming outputs remain in the denominator and score zero.

For Eager, the paired difference is $+0.8$ points; its lower 95% endpoint is $-2.6$ and clears the $-5$ -point gate. Compact differs by $+2.4$ points, with lower endpoint $-0.9$ . It meets the same criterion (Figure 2a).

In the instrumented primary, Eager saves 46.3k prompt tokens per task, or 33.9%; the paired interval ranges from 28.8k to 65.4k saved. Compact saves 28.2% across all attempts. Its 99 runtime-complete pairs save 39.8k tokens on average, with endpoints at 21.6k and 58.0k saved. The useful comparison for history reduction is Compact against its retrieval-matched Eager control. Compact uses 8.5% more prompt tokens, 13.3% more calls, 8.2% more wall time, and 9.4% more energy. Its requests are not longer: dividing prompt volume by successful calls gives at most 10.3k tokens per call for Compact and 10.8k for Eager. Prefix caching is off in this matrix, so the extra calls account for the gap. The anchor drops the remaining candidates, and the agent may search again for evidence that Eager still shows; traces do not label call intent, so this attribution remains open.

### 4.2 RQ2: Physical Savings Follow Fewer Calls

For all four primary cost metrics, the intervals for both policies exclude zero (Figure 2b). Normalizing energy by full-recall localizations yields 3.00, 1.98, and 2.27 kJ for Grep, Eager, and Compact. The quality-adjusted ordering therefore matches the per-attempt ordering (Table 1).

Aggregate energy divided by wall time stays within 27.7–29.3 W in the primary and 25.2–26.0 W in the SGLang stack, so energy mainly tracks duration; calls, uncached prefill, and KV time-area show why costs differ. Mean TTFT varies by less than 2%, and latency per successful call rises from 5.218 to 5.721 seconds (Eager) and 5.468 (Compact), so the task-time saving comes from fewer calls. Peak-KV and system-memory changes are too noisy to support a capacity claim (Appendix A).

#### Failures.

One MicroPython Compact task fails in all repetitions because 61,441 prompt plus 4,096 output tokens exceed the server’s context limit by one; KV memory never runs out. The headline retains its 1.204M failed-request tokens: 98.2k per attempt and 28.2% savings. Removing that charge gives 95.1k over 297 completed cells and 30.5% savings.

#### Build Cost and Cache Isolation.

Compiling the 25 repository indexes takes 767.7 seconds and 36.1 kJ, producing 147,387 chunks in 731 MB. At ten queries per snapshot, amortization adds 3.07 seconds and 0.144 kJ per query; at 100 queries its energy share is below 1.1%.

In the 600-cell cache intervention, turning caching on changes Eager’s logical prompt by $+8.3$ % (95% CI [ $-5.7$ , $+24.7$ ]) but its uncached prefill by $-67.7$ % ([ $-71.0$ , $-63.8$ ]). The planned $C_{\mathrm{loc}}-E_{\mathrm{loc}}$ cache interaction is $-7.1$ k uncached tokens per task; its 95% interval runs from $-17.3$ k to $+2.3$ k. The wall interaction is $+0.1$ seconds, ranging from $-5.4$ to $+5.7$ . Both interaction intervals include zero. The same-model cache-on Compact contrast against Grep is $-38.2$ % uncached prefill, so the $+5.2\%$ increase in the exploratory Qwen3.8/SGLang stack (Table 4) does not reproduce.

Audits confirm that all 100 no-seed cells received no seed and all 300 preload cells match the frozen candidate and query hashes. Trajectory changes may also contribute to the observed resource differences.

## 5 Implications for Resource-Aware Context Management

#### Separate Evidence Delivery from Retention (C1).

Eager uses the fewest resources among eligible localization arms. The anchor remains eligible but adds no saving, because shorter requests do not offset its additional calls.

#### Measure Prefix Reuse (C2).

Equation (1) also locates the break-even point for history deletion: a policy lowers uncached prefill only if it removes more logical tokens than reused ones. Mask-5 removes 75.1k and loses 135.9k. As a first-order estimate, if a runtime served a fraction $\rho$ of the hits observed here in both arms, masking would change uncached prefill by $-75.1\mathrm{k}+135.9\mathrm{k}\cdot\rho$ tokens per attempt, which turns positive above $\rho\approx 0.55$ . At $\rho=0$ , without a prefix cache, masking would save prefill; batching or cache pressure that evicts prefixes lowers $\rho$ and with it the masking penalty. Reports should therefore expose request count, prefix reuse, and uncached prefill alongside prompt volume.

#### Constrain Quality Before Comparing Resources (C3).

Apply Equation (6) before interpreting resource differences. $E_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{loc}}$ meet it against $G$ , while $M_{5}$ does not meet it against $E_{\mathrm{patch}}$ ; token count alone would favor the policy that the gate excludes. Other patch contrasts remain descriptive.

## 6 Related Work

#### Repository Localization and Agent Context.

BugLocator first combined report–code similarity with development history [1]; BLUiR then indexed code structure explicitly [2], and learning-to-rank incorporated API, history, and method features [3]. RepoCoder moved repository retrieval into an iterative generation loop [4], while RepoBench measured broader repository context [33]. SWE-bench made localization an upstream step in executable issue resolution [29]. AutoCodeRover exposed AST-aware search [5]; Agentless used hierarchical file-to-function localization [6]. LocAgent, CoSIL, RepoGraph, and CodexGraph navigate repository code graphs [8, 9, 10, 11]; OrcaLoca prioritizes search actions and prunes context by code distance [7]. We adopt the resulting function/class endpoint, freeze retrieval, and study the resources used to deliver and retain evidence.

Static prompt compression precedes long-horizon agent memory [13, 14]. Later policies externalize memory, mask or summarize observations, prune lines, and maintain structured state [34, 16, 15, 35, 17, 36]. Repository compression also varies by task [37].

#### Runtime Context and KV Reuse.

PagedAttention allocates KV blocks; RadixAttention, Prompt Cache, RAGCache, and CacheBlend reuse state [21, 22, 18, 38, 19]. CacheGen transfers compressed state, while H2O, StreamingLLM, and SnapKV retain selected tokens [39, 40, 41, 42]. ContextPilot aligns reusable context; Stream2LLM models updates that invalidate cache [43, 44]. KV compression can also lengthen outputs and latency [45]. We measure how context policies interact with this reuse.

#### Resource-Aware Evaluation.

Green AI and HELM motivate cost-aware, multi-metric evaluation; Zeus measures GPU energy directly [46, 47, 48]. Our protocol adds a prespecified quality gate, uncached prefill, and KV time-area to these metrics and charges failures and index construction.

## 7 Limitations and Conclusion

Results cover two stacks on one DGX Spark serving one request at a time; batching, cache pressure, and cloud GPUs remain untested. The Spark exposes no application-clock or power-limit control (power.limit=N/A), so clocks were not pinned; Latin-square interleaving spreads drift across policies, and average power stays nearly constant across arms. Server, KV, and energy intervals use only three shards. Quality and detailed cost come from different localization cohorts (450 and 100 tasks), so no single issue set carries both measurements. The patch study covers 100 Python tasks from 12 repositories, with physical intervals over eight shards. Powered localization has one trajectory per policy per repository. The 32-call patch cap measures fixed-budget performance, not unrestricted SWE-bench ability. We test four fixed policies; Mask-5 fixes the window at five observations, following the SWE-agent reference. Window sweeps, LLM summarization, learned pruning, and external memory remain unmeasured, although Equation (1) applies to each. Mini-SWE-agent lacks observation tags; SGLang reports only full-attention KV occupancy. Our GPU proxy omits CPU, host-memory, and whole-system energy. On-device execution retains source privacy, but cheaper misuse and incorrect patches remain risks requiring sandboxing and human review.

#### Conclusion.

A context policy changes both what the agent does and how much of its prompt the runtime can reuse. Early evidence saved work by avoiding calls, while repeated observation masking turned a 33.3% prompt saving into a 608.5% rise in uncached prefill. Resource comparisons should measure executed work and admit only policies that pass a quality gate.

The run sequence is: (1) rebuild or verify repository artifacts; (2) validate the three arms on two tasks and audit compaction traces; (3) perform unmeasured model warm-up; (4) execute three repository shards in rotated policy order; (5) repeat the rotation twice; and (6) bootstrap paired task differences by repository. A shard is invalidated if another client uses the model endpoint, the model process restarts, telemetry has a gap longer than two sampling intervals, or memory pressure triggers swapping. Invalidated shards remain disclosed before reruns; no shard is deleted.

The post-run audit resolves and verifies all 897 persisted traces. It retains a failed status for the other three cells because the exception serializer omits their preload-candidate hash along with the final trace record. Those are the same disclosed context-limit failures; their task and candidate set remain fixed by the selection manifest. We preserve this secondary audit failure without rewriting raw artifacts.

For energy, samples $(t_{i},P_{i})$ are integrated as

$$ E_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{i}\frac{P_{i}+P_{i+1}}{2}(t_{i+1}-t_{i}),\qquad E_{\mathrm{proxy}}=E_{\mathrm{raw}}-\bar{P}_{\mathrm{idle}}\Delta t. $$

Negative idle-subtracted values remain measurement noise in the statistical input; no sample is silently clipped. Whole-system energy requires an external power meter and is outside the primary protocol.

Formal primary and exploratory matrices consume 14.11 and 4.23 measured device-hours, respectively. Compilation adds 0.213 hours. The same-model cache intervention adds 7.90 device-hours across 150 telemetry blocks, while external mini-SWE-agent generation adds 14.65 device-hours across 32 blocks. Their idle-subtracted GPU-energy proxies are 0.183 and 0.281 kWh, respectively. These two added studies therefore account for 22.55 device-hours and 0.464 kWh; official SWE-bench grading is excluded. The accounting excludes model-server residency and other uninstrumented development. A normal DGX Spark graphics session (Xorg and the desktop compositor) remained resident throughout; the idle window captures that background. Only the agent target and embedding containers issued compute requests during formal shards, and neither endpoint received an external client request.

For the exploratory cached-stack probe, all nine Radix-cache resets return HTTP 200, all 300 cells complete, the maximum one-second telemetry gap is 1.16 seconds, and no request queues or swap growth occur. Each arm records nonzero DFlash verification calls. The four-task smoke test is not used as paper evidence.

The external E2E protocol uses the same cached target, draft model, retrieval service, and 65,536-token server limit. It runs Mini, Eager, Compact, and Mask-5 over eight near-equal shards. Every arm occupies each order position twice, and the Radix cache is reset before every policy–shard block. The generation limit is 32 model calls. Official AMD64 grading is excluded from generation-resource totals, while empty patches and test failures remain in the 100-instance denominator.

One pre-execution sandbox check rejected an empty, uninitialized Astropy gitlink. We quarantined and invalidated its entire 13-cell Eager block, including 277 requests and 20.8 measured minutes, then repeated the block after a fresh cache reset. The recovery permits only revision-bound gitlinks whose worktree directories are empty and uninitialized; networking remains disabled. Artifact-preserved copies of the failed cell, discarded telemetry, run manifest, predictions, and original pipeline status remain outside every aggregate.

The Qwen3.8 target and DFlash draft checkpoints also use Apache-2.0, and the SWE-rebench V2 dataset is CC-BY-4.0. Each of the 25 evaluated repositories retains its individual upstream license and pinned commit. To avoid relicensing source-derived index contents, the artifact can distribute manifests and rebuild scripts without bundling the compiled vectors. Code and artifacts are released at https://github.com/sysevol-ai/CodeNib.
